name: confirmation
quote: That's just what thought it would do.
description: Verifying that one's inner prediction model aligns with what's perceived.
perceptions: What I perceived matches the expectation.
results: Most of the time confirming unconscious expectations creates no sensation.
If there was doubt, then we may actually notice something.
examples: getting the birthday present you'd hoped for
a sniffle turned into a flu

comparisons.description: When working through something unknown, confirming various parts is progress, but you may not be _certain_ about the entire outcome until all pieces are seen clearly.
'Validation' is form of social confirmation. In general, 'confirmation' can be about anything.

variations.name: confirmation bias
variations.description: The brain's tendency to favor perceptions that support existing expectations while ignoring perceptions that conflict with expectations.
perceptions: The nature of biases is that you will only perceive them after being confronted with something direct.
results: If your expectations are shown to be wrong, then you're not going to have the level of control and agency desired. So your brain may hide some prediction errors.

guidance.description: Confirmation bias can be reduced with interventions that range from simple decision strategies to more intensive training interventions. A simple strategy one can apply immediately is when testing a hypothesis, make sure to test if alternatives or its negative are true.

examples: Some aspect of events confirm your political views, while other aspects are conveniently ignored.

commentaries.quote: We unconsciously confirm thousands of little expectations every day: the car is in the driveway, the morning is hectic, traffic is bad, coffee is good, etc. Most of the time we only notice when something is not confirmed.

Ignoring contradicting evidence is a key aspect of confirmation bias, but why do we do it? There are several potential reasons: cognitive discomfort, social conformity, wishful thinking, a desire for simplicity, threat to self-identity.
The man of science has learned to believe in justification, not by faith, but by verification.
The doctrine of waiting for confirmation is one of the greatest time killers.
